Keywords: icon button, aria-label, screen reader, accessible name, toolbar, close button
Description: A button that shows only a glyph has no text for a screen reader to speak, so it is announced as just 'button'. The name has to come from markup, not from the picture.
Do: Give every icon-only control a short verb phrase as its accessible name, and mark the SVG itself as hidden from the tree.
Don't: Do not rely on a tooltip, a title attribute or the file name of the icon to name a control.
Code Example Good: <button type='button' aria-label='Close dialog'><svg aria-hidden='true' focusable='false' viewBox='0 0 24 24'><path d='M6 6l12 12M18 6L6 18'/></svg></button>

Keywords: label, input, for attribute, placeholder, accessible name, form field
Description: A placeholder disappears as soon as someone types and is not a reliable name for the field. Each input needs a label that stays on screen and is tied to it in markup.
Do: Wrap or link a visible label to every field; keep hint text in a separate element referenced by aria-describedby.
Don't: Do not use the placeholder as the only label, and do not leave a label unconnected to its input.
Code Example Good: We only use it to send your receipt.

Issue: Role, name and state of custom controls
Keywords: custom control, aria-expanded, aria-pressed, role, native element, disclosure, toggle
Description: A div with a click handler has no role, cannot be focused and says nothing about whether it is open or on. A native element brings all three for free.
Do: Start from button, a, input or details; add aria-expanded or aria-pressed only to reflect real state that your script keeps in sync.
Don't: Do not build buttons from divs or spans, and do not set an ARIA state you never update.
Code Example Good: ...

Keywords: live region, aria-live, status message, toast, async result, screen reader
Description: Content that changes without a page load, such as 'Saved' or '3 results', is silent to a screen reader unless it lives in a live region that was already on the page.
Do: Keep one polite status region in the page from the start and write the message into it; use assertive only for errors that block work.
Don't: Do not inject a brand-new live region together with its text, and do not move focus just to announce a success.

Keywords: decorative, alt text, aria-hidden, svg, redundant icon, screen reader noise
Description: An icon sitting next to a text label repeats what the label says. Read aloud twice, it slows people who navigate by listening.
Do: Use an empty alt on purely decorative img elements and aria-hidden on inline SVG that duplicates adjacent text.
Don't: Do not hide an image that carries information nobody else supplies, and do not write alt text that only says 'icon'.
Code Example Good: Cart (2)

Keywords: tap target, hit area, 44px, 24px, finger, button size, mobile
Description: Fingers are far less exact than a cursor. WCAG 2.2 sets 24 by 24 CSS px as the floor and Apple and Material both advise roughly 44 pt and 48 dp.
Do: Make the interactive area at least 44 by 44 CSS px on touch screens; enlarge the hit area with padding or a pseudo-element when the icon must stay small.
Don't: Do not shrink a control to the size of its glyph, and do not let the small visual size set the clickable size.
Code Example Good: .icon-btn { min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px; display: inline-grid; place-items: center; }

Keywords: tap spacing, adjacent buttons, mis-tap, gap, toolbar, destructive next to safe
Description: Two small controls pressed together invite the wrong tap, which hurts most when one of them deletes something.
Do: Leave at least 8 px between adjacent targets and keep a destructive action away from the common one.
Don't: Do not stack a delete icon directly against edit, and do not rely on users to zoom in.
Code Example Good: .row-actions { display: flex; gap: 12px; } .row-actions .danger { margin-inline-start: 24px; }

Keywords: swipe, touch-action, scroll, pan, horizontal carousel, edge swipe, browser back gesture
Description: A horizontal swipe handler inside a scrolling page fights the browser, and a swipe from the screen edge is often claimed by the system for back navigation.
Do: Declare which gestures your element owns with touch-action, keep custom swipes away from the screen edge, and always give a button route to the same result.
Don't: Do not call preventDefault on every touchmove, and do not start a drawer drag at x = 0.
Code Example Good: .carousel { overflow-x: auto; touch-action: pan-x pan-y; scroll-snap-type: x mandatory; overscroll-behavior-x: contain; }

Keywords: history, back, pushState, single page app, deep link, url, router
Description: People press back to undo a step, not to leave the site. A step that does not change the URL, or one that traps them, breaks that habit.
Do: Give each meaningful screen its own URL through the router and use replace for steps that should not be revisited.
Don't: Do not rewrite history on load to block back, and do not hold a flow's state only in memory.
Code Example Good:
history.pushState({ step: 2 }, '', '/checkout/payment'); // a new screen
history.replaceState(null, '', '/checkout/review'); // a correction
Code Example Bad: history.pushState(null, '', location.href); // trap: undo the back press

Keywords: tab bar, bottom nav, three to five destinations, labels, mobile navigation
Description: A bottom bar works for a few top-level places used often. Beyond five, labels shrink and each target gets too small to hit.
Do: Use three to five destinations with a text label under each icon; mark the current one with more than colour.
Don't: Do not use the bar for actions, and do not hide the labels to fit a sixth item.
Code Example Good: HomeSearchInbox

Keywords: dialog, modal, escape key, close button, focus trap, backdrop
Description: A modal that traps people must also let them out: the Escape key, a visible close control and a return of focus to what opened it.
Do: Use the native dialog element with showModal, a visible Close button and let Escape work; focus returns to the trigger on close.
Don't: Do not build a full-screen overlay with no exit, and do not disable Escape on a dismissible dialog.
Code Example Good: Discard changes?

Keywords: scroll position, back navigation, restore, form draft, list filters, session
Description: Coming back to a list should land where the person left it, with the filters and scroll they had, not a fresh top of page.
Do: Keep filters and page in the URL, let the browser restore scroll, and save long form drafts in sessionStorage.
Don't: Do not reset a list on every visit, and do not lose typed text when a tab is refreshed.
Code Example Good:
history.scrollRestoration = 'auto';
const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search); // filters live in the URL

Keywords: skeleton, spinner, aria-busy, progress, wait, 300ms, placeholder
Description: Under about a second a spinner is only a flicker; beyond that people need to know something is happening and roughly how long.
Do: Show a skeleton shaped like the final content after a short delay and mark the region aria-busy while it loads.
Don't: Do not freeze the screen with no sign of work, and do not flash a spinner for a 100 ms request.

Keywords: success message, toast, saved, confirmation, status, inline feedback
Description: People need to know an action worked, close to where they did it, and not only by a colour change.
Do: Show a short message next to the control or in a status region, saying what happened and what comes next.
Don't: Do not use a toast that vanishes before it can be read, and do not signal success by colour alone.
Code Example Good: Saved at 14:02

Keywords: error, validation message, aria-invalid, retry, plain language, inline error
Description: An error has to say what went wrong, where, and how to fix it, in text that is attached to the field and not only red.
Do: Write the message beside the field, link it with aria-describedby, set aria-invalid and move focus to the first problem on submit.
Don't: Do not show a generic 'Something went wrong', and do not clear what the person typed.
Code Example Good: Enter an age between 18 and 120.

Keywords: inline validation, blur, on submit, premature error, input events
Description: An error shown while someone is still typing their first character feels like scolding. Wait until the field is left, then re-check on each change.
Do: Validate on blur for the first time, then live while the field is invalid; show a summary after a failed submit.
Don't: Do not flag a field on the first keystroke, and do not block submission silently.
Code Example Good: field.addEventListener('blur', check, { once: true }); field.addEventListener('input', () => field.ariaInvalid === 'true' && check());

Keywords: inputmode, type email, tel, numeric keypad, mobile keyboard, enterkeyhint
Description: The on-screen keyboard follows the input type. The right one saves a mode switch for every field.
Do: Choose type and inputmode to match the data: email, tel, url, or numeric for codes.
Don't: Do not use type='number' for card numbers, phone numbers or postcodes.
Code Example Good: <input type='text' inputmode='numeric' autocomplete='one-time-code' pattern='[0-9]{6}'>

Keywords: autocomplete, enterkeyhint, tab order, autofill, address, name
Description: Browsers can fill most personal fields if you name them with autocomplete tokens, and the keyboard's action key can say Next or Done.
Do: Add autocomplete tokens and enterkeyhint, and keep DOM order the same as the visual order.
Don't: Do not turn autocomplete off to be safe, and do not reorder fields with positive tabindex values.
Code Example Good: <input name='fn' autocomplete='given-name' enterkeyhint='next'><input name='ln' autocomplete='family-name' enterkeyhint='done'>

Keywords: password, show password, toggle visibility, paste, password manager
Description: Typing a long secret blind on a small keyboard causes errors. A toggle lets people check it, and allowing paste lets a manager do the work.
Do: Offer a labelled show/hide button with aria-pressed and allow paste and autofill.
Don't: Do not block paste and do not show the password by default.
Code Example Good: <input id='pw' type='password' autocomplete='current-password'><button type='button' aria-pressed='false' aria-controls='pw'>Show password</button>

Keywords: virtual list, content-visibility, windowing, scroll jank, many rows
Description: Thousands of rendered rows slow layout and memory. Skipping off-screen work keeps scrolling smooth.
Do: Paginate, window the list, or let the browser skip off-screen rows with content-visibility and a size hint.
Don't: Do not render an unbounded list in one go.
Code Example Good: .row { content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 64px; }

Keywords: srcset, sizes, width height, lazy loading, layout shift, responsive images
Description: A desktop-size image on a phone wastes bytes, and an image with no dimensions pushes text around as it loads.
Do: Give images width and height, serve sizes through srcset, and lazy-load those below the fold.
Don't: Do not lazy-load the main hero image, and do not ship one huge file for every screen.

Keywords: scroll handler, resize, passive listener, requestAnimationFrame, debounce, throttle
Description: Scroll and pointer events fire many times per frame. Heavy work in each one blocks painting and makes the page feel stuck.
Do: Mark scroll and touch listeners passive and batch visual work into one requestAnimationFrame callback.
Don't: Do not read layout and write styles inside every scroll event.
Code Example Good:
let queued = false;
addEventListener('scroll', () => { if (queued) return; queued = true; requestAnimationFrame(() => { queued = false; update(); }); }, { passive: true });

Keywords: transition, 200ms, ease-out, duration, micro-interaction, timing
Description: Interface feedback should feel immediate. Short ease-out transitions make a change legible without making people wait.
Do: Use roughly 100 to 250 ms for small state changes with an ease-out curve; longer only for large surfaces.
Don't: Do not animate with linear for entrances, and do not run routine feedback for half a second.
Code Example Good: .menu { transition: opacity 160ms cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), transform 160ms cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1); }

Keywords: prefers-reduced-motion, vestibular, motion sickness, accessibility, animation off
Description: Large movement can cause dizziness or nausea for some people. The operating-system setting tells you to tone it down.
Do: Wrap movement in a media query that removes travel and keeps a short fade that still shows the change.
Don't: Do not ignore the preference, and do not remove the state change itself.
Code Example Good: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .panel { transition: opacity 120ms; transform: none; } }

Keywords: infinite animation, pause, autoplay, marquee, attention, spinner
Description: Anything that keeps moving competes with the task and can distract. WCAG asks for a way to stop motion that runs longer than five seconds.
Do: Run loops only while something is loading, and give a pause control to any decorative or autoplaying movement.
Don't: Do not leave several infinite animations running on one screen.
Code Example Good: .loading::after { animation: spin 1s linear infinite; } .loading[hidden]::after { animation: none; }
Code Example Bad: .card { animation: pulse 2s infinite; } .badge { animation: bounce 1s infinite; }

Keywords: 16px, iOS zoom, body text, readable, input font size, mobile type
Description: Body text under about 16 px is tiring on a phone, and Safari on iPhone zooms into any form field smaller than 16 px.
Do: Set body and form controls to at least 16 px, expressed in rem, with a line height around 1.5.
Don't: Do not shrink input text to 13 px to fit a layout.
Code Example Good: html { font-size: 100%; } body { font: 1rem/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif; } input, select, textarea { font-size: 1rem; }

Keywords: dynamic type, text resize, zoom, rem, 200 percent, large text
Description: People change their default text size in the browser or the OS. Pixel-locked boxes then clip or overlap.
Do: Size type and its containers in rem and em, let heights grow, and test at 200 percent.
Don't: Do not fix a height on any box that holds text.
Code Example Good: .btn { font-size: 1rem; padding: .75em 1.25em; min-height: 2.75rem; }

Keywords: notch, safe area, env(), viewport-fit cover, home indicator, bottom bar
Description: Phones have notches and gesture bars. Content or tap targets under them are hidden or hard to press.
Do: Opt in with viewport-fit=cover and pad fixed bars with env(safe-area-inset-*).
Don't: Do not fix a toolbar flush to the bottom without padding for the home indicator.
Code Example Good:
<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover'>
.bar { padding-bottom: max(12px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)); }

Keywords: dark mode, contrast, prefers-color-scheme, 4.5:1, theme, colour tokens
Description: A palette that passes on white may fail on dark. Each theme needs its own checked pair of text and background.
Do: Define colours as tokens per scheme and check text at 4.5:1 and UI edges at 3:1 in both.
Don't: Do not just invert colours, and do not use pure grey text on a dark card.
Code Example Good: :root { --bg: #fff; --fg: #1a1a1a; } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --bg: #14161a; --fg: #ececec; } }

Keywords: swipe to delete, long press, hidden action, discoverability, alternative
Description: A swipe or long press is invisible and impossible for some people to perform. Every gesture needs a visible control that does the same.
Do: Offer a menu or button for each gesture-driven action and keep keyboard access.
Don't: Do not hide delete, archive or reorder behind a gesture only.
Code Example Good: • Invoice 204

Keywords: drag and drop, reorder, sortable, single pointer, move up down
Description: Dragging needs steady fine movement. WCAG 2.2 requires a way to do the same job with simple taps.
Do: Add up and down buttons or a move menu next to any draggable item.
Don't: Do not make drag the only way to reorder.
Code Example Good: • Task A

Keywords: login, paste, password manager, one-time code, cognitive test, captcha
Description: Remembering or retyping a secret is a barrier for many people. Let tools do it for them.
Do: Allow paste, support password managers with autocomplete tokens and offer links or passkeys as an alternative.
Don't: Do not require transcribing a code from a picture with no alternative.
Code Example Good: <input name='code' inputmode='numeric' autocomplete='one-time-code'>

Keywords: overscroll-behavior, scroll chaining, pull refresh, modal scroll lock, bounce
Description: Scrolling past the end of an inner panel can scroll the page beneath, or trigger a refresh by accident.
Do: Contain scrolling inside sheets and menus with overscroll-behavior.
Don't: Do not lock the body with fixed positioning hacks that lose scroll place.
Code Example Good: .sheet-body { overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior: contain; }

Issue: Focus not hidden by sticky bars
Keywords: focus obscured, sticky header, scroll-padding, keyboard focus, fixed bar
Description: A fixed header or cookie bar can cover the element that keyboard focus just landed on.
Do: Add scroll-padding equal to the bar height so focused items scroll clear of it.
Don't: Do not rely on mouse users to notice.
Code Example Good: html { scroll-padding-top: 4.5rem; } .site-header { position: sticky; top: 0; height: 4rem; }
Code Example Bad: .site-header { position: fixed; top: 0; height: 4rem; } /* nothing offsets focus */

Keywords: offline, navigator.onLine, retry, queued, connection lost, sync
Description: Mobile connections come and go. Say what is stored locally and what is waiting to send.
Do: Show a persistent offline notice, keep user input, and retry when the connection returns.
Don't: Do not show a blank screen or lose a drafted message.
Code Example Good: addEventListener('offline', () => banner.hidden = false); addEventListener('online', () => { banner.hidden = true; flushQueue(); });

Keywords: delete, undo, confirm, irreversible, snackbar, danger button
Description: Deleting by mistake costs people work. Undo is kinder than a confirmation that everyone clicks through.
Do: Offer undo for reversible deletes; for irreversible ones, name the thing in the confirmation and label the button with the verb.
Don't: Do not use a generic 'Are you sure? OK / Cancel'.
Code Example Good: Delete the project 'Spring menu'? This cannot be undone.

Keywords: empty state, no results, first use, call to action, zero data
Description: A blank list reads like a bug. An empty screen should say why it is empty and what to do next.
Do: Explain what will appear, and give one clear action.
Don't: Do not show a bare table header with no rows.
Code Example Good:
No invoices yet

Invoices you send appear here.

Create an invoice

Keywords: permission, notifications, location, camera, prompt, just in time
Description: A permission request on first load, with no reason given, is usually refused, and a refusal is hard to undo.
Do: Ask right after an action that needs it, with a sentence first saying why.
Don't: Do not request notifications or location on page load.
Code Example Good: <button id='loc'>Find stores near me</button><script>loc.onclick = () => navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(show, fail);</script>
